title: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says
content:
The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.
It will be replaced by a spin-off show featuring highlights from past episodes. Sources denied reports in the Sun newspaper the programme would be axed as part of a plan to make savings.
Presented by Nick Knowles, DIY SOS sees a team transform the homes of families who are facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.
It was first broadcast in 1999 and is currently airing its 35th series on BBC One and iPlayer.
The decision comes during the corporation's drive to save £500m over three years. It has already cancelled several well-known TV shows including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.
A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC's savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore.
"DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show's past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year."
After initially concentrating on small-scale renovations, DIY SOS shifted focus to tackle a number of more ambitious projects throughout its multiple-decade run.
Among them was a 2015 special that saw hundreds of volunteers work alongside Knowles, Prince William and Prince Harry to build housing for veterans in Manchester.
William returned to the programme in 2018 for a two-part special supporting survivors and the community affected by the Grenfell Tower fire.
The emotional episodes saw the team build a new community centre and restore the Dale Youth Boxing Club, which was destroyed in the disaster.
The programme's latest episode saw the team overhaul a family's property to allow their 17-year-old son Dan - who has complex disabilities - to receive treatment at home after spending more than three years in hospital.
Dan's father, Nigel, told the BBC it was a "miracle".

final_quality.reason: This article reports a substantive category-specific development, namely the decision to 'rest' a long-running TV series and replace it with a spin-off show, providing a clear reason for readers to care. The article also provides context about the show's impact and the BBC's drive to save £500m over three years.

title: From fan art to Star Wars: The poster artist behind Marvel and Disney hits
content:
A film fan who began creating his own movie poster artwork for fun has gone on to work on some of Hollywood's biggest franchises, including  Marvel, Indiana Jones and Star Wars.
Paul Shipper said he was spotted after sharing designs online, leading to opportunities that once felt like "a dream", inspired by the films of George Lucas and Steven Spielberg.
Among the projects he has worked on are posters and artwork for blockbuster titles including Avengers: Infinity War, Doctor Strange, Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, Star Wars: The Last Jedi, Obi-Wan Kenobi and Skeleton Crew.
The illustrator said becoming a movie poster artist had originally seemed a long way off, before the early days of the internet helped his work find an audience.
"It was just through kind of sheer dumb luck really and the internet that it happened," he said.
"Before you know it, there are people who see it who are connected with the movies and then all of a sudden you get asked if you're interested in working on a Steven Spielberg movie or something like that."
Shipper described himself as "a Spielberg and George Lucas kid", saying franchises such as Star Wars and Indiana Jones were the films that first inspired him to become an illustrator.
For Shipper, the appeal of poster art lies in being able to tell a story with a single image.
"You're trying to distill something within one image," he said.
"It is kind of like a trailer... there are posters that tell you too much, so there is a fine line."
Shipper, who primarily works with pencils, said every commission presents a different creative challenge.
Looking back over his career, however, he was struck by how consistent his artistic style had remained, despite working across a wide variety of projects.
He said he thought his work had earned recognition among collectors and film fans partly because it drew on the tradition of the illustrated movie posters that were once a familiar sight outside cinemas and in video rental shops.
Gareth Griffiths, founder of AMPjam Poster Convention, said Shipper was among a small number of artists still working in a style associated with some of cinema's most iconic promotional artwork.
"He is one of precious few people that the film studio could go to if they're looking for someone that creates in that classic 70s and 80s style," Griffiths said.
The pair are now involved in AMPjam Presents: We've Been Framed, a charity exhibition bringing together more than 60 artists from around the world.
Many are known for creating alternative movie posters, which offer fresh artistic interpretations of films rather than reproducing the original cinema artwork.
The show is currently running at The Jointworks in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter and features original artworks inspired by films and television shows including Jurassic Park, Star Wars, Toy Story, The Lord of the Rings, Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory and Lilo & Stitch.
Their concept turns a traditional exhibition on its head, the pair said, with artists creating original pieces inspired by a film or television show and designing them to fit unusual vintage or repurposed frames.
More than 60 one-off works have been produced by movie poster artists from around the world.

final_quality.reason: A behind-the-scenes look at the life of a movie poster artist who has worked on prominent franchises like Marvel, Indiana Jones, and Star Wars, providing a unique perspective on the creative process and the evolution of the artist's style.
